extracted.intended_audience: educators, educational theorists, school administrators, and teachers
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for designing and evaluating moral education in schools focused on linking knowledge, activity, and social life so that learning shapes character and conduct. Emphasizes pragmatic continuity between experience, interest, and cooperative occupations rather than isolated catechesis or formal discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge as organized dispositions (pragmatic conception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge consists of our intellectual resources — of all the habits that render our action intelligent; only that which has been organized into our disposition so as to enable us to adapt the environment to our needs and to adapt our aims and desires to the situation in which we live is really knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat knowing not as mere conscious facts but as dispositions and habits used in practical adaptation. Evaluate whether learning produces dispositions that students can bring to consciousness to resolve practical perplexities and modify the environment. Anti-pattern: valuing only verbal acquaintance or fleeting consciousness of facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity of learning with activity and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral education requires a consecutive activity embodying the student's own interest, where a definite result is to be obtained, and where neither routine habit nor following dictated directions nor capricious improvising will suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design curricular tasks that have identifiable outcomes and require reflection and purposive effort. Assess whether students' activities demand deliberation and adaptation rather than rote performance. Examples: occupations, projects, cooperative tasks with real consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: School as a community life
rubrics_metrics.description: The school must itself be a community life in all which that implies. Social perceptions and interests can be developed only in a genuinely social medium—one where there is give and take in the building up of a common experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure school organization, routines, and spaces (playgrounds, shops, workrooms, laboratories) support interpersonal cooperation, communication, and shared responsibility. Anti-pattern: isolated, individualistic classroom work that lacks social interchange.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning continuous with out-of-school life
rubrics_metrics.description: The learning in school should be continuous with that out of school. There should be a free interplay between the two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create points of contact between school activities and community/home life so skills, interests, and social responsibilities transfer beyond the school. Beware academic seclusion or an idealized past that makes school life inapplicable to present social concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of inner motive and outer conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject sharp demarcation between motive/character (inner) and conduct/consequences (outer); conscious deliberation and desire are phases of continuous activity that culminate in overt action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame moral education so that reflection and feeling are connected to observable action and consequences. Avoid treating 'meaning well' as sufficient without providing opportunities for thought to issue into action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding the duty vs. interest false dichotomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Acting from 'principle' and acting from 'interest' are not rigid opposites if the self is seen as forming through action; interest in an occupation is the continuity that sustains persistence and moral conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foster pupils' interest in the continuous development of occupations so duty becomes part of sustained engagement rather than an abstract injunction. Evaluate whether pupils persist through obstacles because of interest, not merely external enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-hand, experience-based knowledge over second-hand recitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge gained at first hand through the exigencies of experience is the kind that affects conduct; second-handed, symbolic recognition (mere information) has limited moral influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize experiential, practice-oriented learning that ties understanding to action. Assess whether student knowledge is tested and internalized through doing, not only through recitation or memorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual attitudes as moral traits
rubrics_metrics.description: Open-mindedness, single-mindedness, sincerity, breadth of outlook, thoroughness, assumption of responsibility for consequences — these intellectual qualities are intrinsically moral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate moral education by the extent it cultivates these intellectual habits. Do curricula develop habits of reflection, responsibility, and honest inquiry rather than mere compliance?

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral education through occupations with social ends
rubrics_metrics.description: What is learned and employed in an occupation having an aim and involving cooperation with others is moral knowledge, for it builds up social interest and confers the intelligence needed to make that interest effective in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement cooperative, aim-directed occupations (projects, community tasks) as core pedagogy. Measure moral formation by students' capacity to contribute to shared ends and to assume social responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject scholastic/formal discipline disconnected from experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The scholastic method and doctrine of formal discipline — making distinctions, definitions, divisions, and classifications for the mere sake of making them — is inadequate when disconnected from experience and purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid instructional practices that prioritize abstract formal procedures or 'discipline' for its own sake. Prefer activities where conceptual work arises from and serves practical problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance particularizing and generalizing functions in knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Real knowledge involves particularizing (specifying facts via senses) and generalizing (applying prior experience to give meaning). Both functions must work together to reorganize experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design lessons that help students discriminate particulars and recombine them with prior generalizations; assess whether students can apply generalized meanings to new particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid narrow moralism and catechetical instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct instruction 'about morals' is ineffective in democratic societies unless reinforced by the whole regime; moral training reduced to catechetical lessons risks mere obedience or sentimental magic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use moral instruction embedded in school life and shared activities rather than isolated admonitions or memorized lists of duties. Look for institutional coherence: do routines and authority structures reinforce or contradict taught moral lessons?

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral qualities are holistic and socially integrated
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtues (truthfulness, honesty, chastity, amiability) are central because they carry many connected attitudes; virtue means being fully and adequately what one can become through association with others in the offices of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess moral development by examining whole-character integration and capacity to participate in social life, not by checking off isolated virtues. Favor curricula that cultivate broad social competencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative and curricular worth measured by social spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: The measure of the worth of the administration, curriculum, and methods of instruction of the school is the extent to which they are animated by a social spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate schools on whether policies, curriculum, and pedagogy foster permeating social engagement. A lack of social conditions (isolation of school, separation from life) is the chief enemy of effective moral training.
